query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, conformal interfacial coating (e.g., via atomic layer deposition) onto W particles before copper infiltration and sintering will improve interfacial wetting and bonding, thereby suppressing void formation and phase separation in a W–Cu composite while preserving mechanical durability under fusion‐reactor conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles embedded or intended to be embedded in a Cu matrix, produced by conventional powder approaches that typically show interfacial voids and phase separation.
generation.intervention: Pre-treat W particles with an ALD-deposited, nanometer-scale metallic coating (which could be Cu or a reactive metal that forms a low-melting eutectic with Cu) before copper infiltration and spark plasma sintering.
generation.conditions: Processing under SPS conditions at temperatures below the tungsten melting point (but above Cu melting temperature) with controlled time and temperature; service conditions representative of fusion reactor irradiation and high heat flux.
generation.structural_mediator: A conformal, ultra-thin metallic layer on each W particle that enhances metal–metal contact, reduces interfacial energy and barriers to diffusion, and leads to a continuous, defect-suppressed W–Cu network.
generation.mechanism: The ALD layer promotes improved wetting of molten or sintering copper, enhancing diffusion at the interface and creating a near-perfect metallurgical bond that minimizes the formation of voids and phase-separated regions which are otherwise deleterious to thermal transport and mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline fabricated from uncoated W powders (e.g., via conventional spark plasma sintering), the ALD-coated W–Cu composite is expected to exhibit significantly reduced void content, improved microstructural uniformity, and enhanced thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability.
generation.baseline: Conventional fabrication methods such as spark plasma sintering or mechanical alloying of uncoated W powders in a Cu matrix, which typically suffer from incomplete wetting and void formation.
generation.boundary: The processing window is limited to sintering temperatures that do not cause degradation of the ALD coating; the service conditions are those relevant for high heat load and irradiation in fusion reactor joints. Excessively thick ALD coatings or integration complexities could shift the balance of properties.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal ALD coating material and thickness, as well as the long-term stability of the interfacial layer under fusion irradiation conditions, remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set using W powders with the ALD coating applied and a control set using uncoated W powders. Both sample sets should be processed identically via copper infiltration and spark plasma sintering under conditions optimized for Cu–W composites. Characterize the resulting microstructure (using high-resolution electron microscopy) and measure thermal conductivity and mechanical properties.
measurements: Quantitative porosity and void fraction via image analysis
Interfacial quality assessed by electron microscopy and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX)
Mechanical durability tests under simulated irradiation conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ALD-coated W–Cu samples do not show statistically significant reductions in void formation, improvements in thermal conductivity, and maintain mechanical durability (as compared to the uncoated control samples), then the hypothesis that the ALD coating enhances interfacial bonding and suppresses defects is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: CrMnFeCoNi alloy can be fabricated by either casting (melting and solidification) [,,,], sintering (powder metallurgy) [,,,], or other methods [,,,,]. Compared with the more frequently studied casting, sintering has a great economic advantage in saving materials and energy []. On the other hand, the element distribution in sintered alloys is usually more inhomogeneous than that of casted ones. One example is the Cr, Mn, and O enrichment in spark-plasma-sintered alloys []. The zones with specific element enrichment generally affect the mechanical properties and electrochemical stability. In addition, the impurities of carbon or oxygen from raw powders also play essential roles in the above properties. Therefore, the relationship between the specific microstructure, the mechanical properties, and the electrochemical stability of sintered alloys needs to be sufficiently clarified. Until now, many CrMnFeCoNi alloys have been sintered under specific conditions, and their mechanical properties have been studied [,,,,,,]. A possible way to solve the problem of manufacturing Co-Cr-Cu-Fe-Ni HEAs that would exhibit a combination of excellent mechanical properties is to form the non-cast types of microstructure using alternative technologies for their production (e.g., the methods based on powder metallurgy). It has been demonstrated in refs. [,,] that single-phase CoCrCuxFeNi alloys having a nanocrystalline microstructure can be manufactured employing mechanically alloyed (MA) powder mixtures as starting materials and consolidation methods such as hot pressing (HP) or spark plasma sintering (SPS). The advantages of this technology over casting are as follows. Mechanical alloying can be used to produce solid solutions from metal powders due to high-energy mechanical impacts (multiple collisions with grinding bodies in the milling jars) despite the limitations or even the complete absence of mutual solubility []. The HP and SPS methods are used to consolidate powder materials at temperatures below the melting point of the main components. Therefore, the nanocrystalline microstructure inherited from the MA powders is preserved.

One way to enhance the reactivity of the powder mixture is to activate it by treatment in various apparatuses, mainly planetary mills []. The main difference from the above-mentioned mechanical alloying approach is that mechanical activation (MA) does not last as long and does not lead to the formation of new phases. During MA, the powders are crushed and the surfaces of the particles are cleaned from the oxide films. The contact area between components increases. Often, it allows the decreasing of the initiation temperature and promotes a more complete reaction in mixtures that burn weakly without activation []. Since Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni refers to systems in which SHS is difficult or impossible (depending on the composition), MA can be used to initiate a reaction in them without the use of a thermally coupled reaction. Moreover, preliminary activated powders can be used not only for combustion synthesis, but also for reaction sintering, which is based on the idea of simultaneous synthesis and compaction of the material.
